title: Numbers and math
summary: Arithmetic, the integer-division trap, and shortcuts for updating a value.

steps.title: Arithmetic operators
body: C# does maths with the symbols you expect, plus one you may not know.
Yes: `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. When **both** sides are `int`, the result is an `int` and the fraction is thrown away. `%` gives you what was left over.

steps.explain: 5 goes into 17 three whole times (15), leaving a remainder of 2.

steps.title: Getting the decimal back
body: If **either** side is a `double`, the division keeps its fraction.
`(double)total` is a **cast**: it converts the value to a `double` for this one calculation.
Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, as in school. Use parentheses to change the order: `(2 + 3) * 4` is `20`.

steps.prompt: Is the result a whole number or does it keep a fraction?
steps.explain: In `(double)(5 / 2)` the integer division happens first, inside the parentheses. Converting `2` to a double afterwards cannot bring the fraction back.

steps.title: Updating a variable
body: Changing a variable based on its own value is so common that it has shortcuts.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program prints `12`.
steps.explain: 4, plus 2 is 6, times 2 is 12. Doubling first would give 10.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2.5`.
steps.explain: The variable must be a `double` to hold `2.5`, and one side must be cast so the division is not integer division.

steps.title: Fix the average
steps.prompt: Three test scores average `84.33...`, but this program prints `84`. Fix it so it prints `84.33`. (`Math.Round(value, 2)` rounds to two decimal places and is already there.)
hints: `(a + b + c)` is an `int` and `3` is an `int`, so the division is integer division.
Make one side a `double`: divide by `3.0`, or cast the sum with `(double)`.

steps.title: Two digits, always
body: A timer that shows `1h 2m 5s` looks broken. Clocks pad to two digits: `1h 02m 05s`. In an interpolated string,
a **format** after a colon does that:
Your next two exercises are Sidekick pieces: your code becomes the body of a method, the input is given, and you
put the answer in `result` (as in the last lesson).

steps.title: Minutes to hours and minutes
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the formatter every report uses.** Your code becomes the body of
`static string FormatMinutes(int minutes)`. `minutes` is given; put the text in `result` as hours, `h`, a space,
the minutes padded to two digits, `m`:
starter: // minutes is given. Put e.g. "2h 10m" in result.
template: Dojo.Eq("605 minutes pads the minutes", "10h 05m", FormatMinutes(605));
hints: `minutes / 60` is the whole hours, `minutes % 60` what is left over.

build.title: Minutes formatter
build.unlocks: Every time Sidekick shows minutes, it uses your formatter.
transform: // Minutes formatter: your own passing code from the code-dojo C# track (First steps > Numbers and math).

steps.title: Seconds to a timer
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the running timer.** `sk` keeps seconds; you show them like a stopwatch. Your code becomes the
body of `static string FormatDuration(int seconds)`. `seconds` is given; put `<h>h <mm>m <ss>s` in `result`:
Hours are not limited to 24: a timer left running all weekend should say so.
starter: // seconds is given. Put e.g. "1h 02m 05s" in result.
template: Dojo.Eq("one second short of a day", "23h 59m 59s", FormatDuration(86399));
hints: 3600 seconds make an hour. Integer division tells you how many whole hours fit.
`seconds % 3600` is what is left after the hours; divide that by 60 for minutes. `seconds % 60` is the seconds.
`result = $"{hours}h {minutes:00}m {secs:00}s";` (call your seconds variable something other than `seconds`, which is taken).

build.title: Timer formatter
build.unlocks: `sk` can now show a running timer as 0h 12m 30s.
transform: // Timer formatter: your own passing code from the code-dojo C# track (First steps > Numbers and math).
